name: Node
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Who Actually Runs a Blockchain?
lesson.summary: A node is any computer running blockchain software that participates in the network, and the collective, decentralized activity of many independent nodes, not any single company or server, is what actually keeps a blockchain running.
lesson.body:
Every concept covered so far in this chapter, distributed ledgers, replication, blocks, transactions, has quietly assumed the existence of participants doing the actual work of storing, checking, and passing along data. It is time to name them directly. A node is any individual computer running the blockchain's software and connected to the network of other nodes running the same software. There is no central server that "is" a public blockchain; the blockchain is, in a very literal sense, the collective activity of its nodes.

This builds on peer-to-peer networking covered earlier in this course. In a peer-to-peer network, participants connect directly to one another rather than routing everything through a central server, and each participant can act as both a client requesting information and a server providing it to others. Blockchain nodes work this way: a node connects to a handful of other nodes, called peers, and information, new transactions, newly created blocks, propagates through the network as each node relays what it receives to its own peers, who relay it to theirs, and so on, until it has spread to the whole network.

Nodes vary considerably in what they actually store and check, and this variation matters enormously for how decentralized a network really is in practice, not just in theory. Some nodes store the entire history of the blockchain and independently verify every transaction and every block against the network's rules; the next section covers this category, full nodes, in detail. Other, lighter nodes might store only recent data or only block headers, trusting other nodes for parts of the verification, in exchange for using far less storage and bandwidth. Mining or validating nodes go further still, actively participating in creating new blocks, depending on the network's consensus mechanism.

A concrete way to see why this matters: if a blockchain definition claim, like "this ledger cannot be secretly altered," depended on trusting one specific company's server, it would really just be a database with extra steps, no different in principle from any centralized system, dressed in blockchain vocabulary. What makes the tamper evidence claim credible is that thousands of independently operated nodes, run by different people, in different countries, with no coordination requirement beyond running compatible software, are all separately checking the same rules. An attacker cannot simply compromise one node's copy of the ledger and have that count as the truth, because every other node checking the same data will disagree with the altered copy and reject it.

It is fair to be skeptical about how decentralized this actually is on any given network. Running a full node, as the next section covers, has real costs in storage, bandwidth, and technical setup, which means the number of people who actually run one is often far smaller than the number of people who use the network. A blockchain with technically thousands of nodes but where a handful of large operators, exchanges, or cloud providers run the overwhelming majority of them is more centralized in practice than the raw node count suggests. Counting nodes is a starting point for evaluating decentralization, not the end of the conversation.
